summary: Allen Pike of Forestwalk Labs discusses building voice-in, visuals-out AI experiences, drawing on Andrej Karpathy's argument that voice is humans' preferred input for AIs while visuals are the preferred output. The visuals-out side is intuitive: a third of the brain processes visual information, and modern models can generate rich HTML, use tool calling, produce interactive controls, and even create illustrations. The voice-in side is more controversial. Current voice interfaces like Siri or ChatGPT voice mode are often slow and awkward, making people skeptical. However, speaking conveys more words per minute and richer emotional content than typing, which is why people jump on calls for important communication. Pike shares an example where a Forestwalk voice agent in a call filed a Linear issue within a second of a spoken request, feeling natural and non-interruptive. The primary obstacle is latency. Research since the 1960s shows ~100ms feels instant, ~1000ms is the limit before attention drifts, and ~200ms is needed for seamless voice conversation. Some companies like Thinking Machines and Neolab are exploring time-sliced architectures for voice-in-voice-out, but Pike argues voice-in-visuals-out benefits from a more forgiving visual response envelope—on-screen results within a second feel seamless. He shares three key techniques: first, use a fast Haiku-class model with latency-prioritizing inference (GPT-5 mini showed 5000-10000ms latencies despite being small); heavier work can be handed off asynchronously to a larger model. Second, send inference requests eagerly at 1-2 second intervals during speech rather than waiting for silence. Third, maintain a stable caching regimen using prefix caching, keeping ~90% of the context window stable across requests to achieve up to 90% cheaper and faster inference.

sections.title: Introduction and Karpathy's Argument
sections.summary: Pike introduces himself and cites Andrej Karpathy's argument that voice is the preferred input for AIs and visuals the preferred output, noting recent breakthroughs make this feasible.

sections.title: Visuals Out: Intuitive and Now Capable
sections.summary: Explains why visuals-out is intuitive—a third of the brain processes visual information—and that models can now generate rich HTML, tool calls, interactive controls, and illustrations.

sections.title: Voice In: Controversial but High Bandwidth
sections.summary: Voice input is controversial because existing experiences like Siri and ChatGPT voice mode are slow and dumb. Yet speaking conveys more words per minute and richer emotional content than typing, which is why people prefer calls for important communication. Pike shares Forestwalk's call agent that filed a Linear issue in real time.

sections.title: The Tyranny of Latency
sections.summary: Discusses latency requirements: 100ms feels instant, 1000ms is the attention limit, 200ms is needed for seamless voice conversation. Mentions Thinking Machines and Neolab's time-sliced architecture for voice-in-voice-out, but argues voice-in-visuals-out benefits from a more forgiving sub-second visual response envelope.

sections.title: Technique 1: Use a Fast Model
sections.summary: Recommends a Haiku-class model on a latency-prioritizing platform. GPT-5 mini showed 5000-10000ms latencies despite being small. Heavier work can be handed off asynchronously to a larger model.

sections.title: Technique 2: Short Inference Intervals
sections.summary: Instead of waiting for silence after speech, send inference requests eagerly every 1-2 seconds as the person speaks, creating a more seamless experience.

sections.title: Technique 3: Stable Caching Regimen
sections.summary: Leverage prefix caching by keeping ~90% of the context window stable across requests, varying only the final 10%, and minimizing output tokens for fast, affordable inference.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.summary: Pike invites audience members exploring real-time or boundary-pushing AI experiences to connect and share learnings.

demonstrations: Forestwalk built a voice agent that joins calls and filed a Linear issue within a second of a spoken request
Thinking Machines and Neolab demoed a time-sliced architecture with 200ms chunks for continuous inference
limitations: Voice-in-voice-out demands ~200ms latency, which is extremely difficult to achieve with standard network-inference round trips
GPT-5 mini, despite being a small model, exhibited 5000-10000ms latencies in practice
Waiting for silence after speech blows the latency budget for real-time responses
quantitativeClaims: 100ms response feels instant to humans (known since the 1960s)
1000ms is the limit before people lose their train of thought
200ms or less is needed for seamless voice conversation with interruption and interjection
GPT-5 mini showed 5000-7000ms P95 latency, sometimes 10000ms
Prefix caching can yield up to 90% cheaper and faster inference
Aim for first 90% of context window to be stable, with only final 10% varying
